extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining whether method/process claims are directed to abstract ideas, laws of nature, or transformations (machine-or-transformation test) and for making/relying on prima facie rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101. Covers examination steps, relevant factors, and how to document the analysis on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: "extra-solution" activity means activity that is not central to the purpose of the method invented by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: gathering data to use in the method when all applications of the method would require some form of data gathering would not impose a meaningful limit on the claim. Use this concept to identify machine/apparatus or transformation involvement that is merely nominal or post-solution and therefore weighs against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus (machine-or-transformation clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue, and investigative tool, for determining whether some claimed inventions are processes under § 101." A "machine" is a concrete thing (broadly interpreted to include electrical, electronic, optical, acoustic devices); an "apparatus" can include a machine or group of machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant considerations: the particularity or generality of the elements of the machine or apparatus (specific identification weighs toward eligibility); for computer-implemented processes a general purpose computer may be sufficiently "particular" when programmed to perform the process steps because such programming creates a special purpose computer (citing In re Alappat); however, "adding a 'computer-aided' limitation ... without more, is insufficient" where claims are silent as to how/extent/significance of the computer (DealerTrack). To qualify as a particular machine, the claim must clearly convey that the computer is programmed to perform the steps. If the claim is so abstract and sweeping that performing it would cover substantially all practical applications of a judicial exception, the machine is not sufficiently particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine/apparatus subfactor: Whether the machine implements the steps of the method
rubrics_metrics.description: Integral use of a machine or apparatus to achieve performance of the method weighs toward eligibility, as compared to where the machine or apparatus is merely an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the machine merely serves as the source of data or an object on which steps operate (i.e., cannot perform the claimed steps), that weighs against eligibility (citing Cybersource v. Retail Decisions). The extent of the machine's role — integral vs incidental — is material to the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine/apparatus subfactor: Whether the machine's involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which (or how) the machine or apparatus imposes meaningful limits on execution of the claimed method steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to execution of the method (e.g., in a data gathering step or in a field-of-use limitation) weighs against eligibility. Limiting an abstract idea to one field of use or adding token post-solution components does not make the concept patentable (citing Bilski, Cybersource).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether performance of the claimed method results in or otherwise involves a transformation of a particular article
rubrics_metrics.description: “Transformation and reduction of an article ‘to a different state or thing’ is the clue to patentability of a process claim that does not include particular machines.” An "article" includes a physical object or substance and can include electronic data that represents a physical object or substance (data should be more than an abstract value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation means the article has changed to a different state or thing — usually more than mere use or change of location. A new/different function or use can evidence transformation. Purely mental processes are not an eligible transformation; manipulation of basic mathematical constructs is not a transformation. For electronic data, transformation may be found when the nature of the data is changed so it has a different function or is suitable for a different use (citations: Bilski, Cybersource, Warmerdam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation subfactors (particularity, degree, nature, article type, extrasolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a transformation occurs, consider: (a) particularity vs generality of the transformation; (b) degree to which the recited article is particular; (c) nature/extent of the change (different function/use vs mere location change); (d) nature of the article transformed (object/substance vs concept); (e) whether involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More particular transformations and specifically identified articles weigh toward eligibility. Transformations applied to generically recited articles weigh against eligibility. Transformations that contribute only nominally or insignificantly (e.g., mere data gathering) weigh against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether performance of the claimed method involves an application of a law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An application of a law of nature may represent patent-eligible subject matter even in the absence of a particular machine or transformation. If such an application exists, the claims are less likely to be drawn to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a natural principle is a limiting element, evaluate whether the claim applies that principle in a particular, practical way rather than preempting the principle itself. See MPEP § 2106.01 for more guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-of-nature subfactors (particularity, subjective determination, extrasolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application of a law of nature is present, consider: (a) the particularity or generality of the application (broad applicability across many fields weighs against eligibility); (b) whether the claimed method recites an application solely involving subjective determinations (ways to think about the law) — such recitations weigh against eligibility; (c) whether the application's involvement is extrasolution activity or a field-of-use (nominal contribution weighs against eligibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that would monopolize a natural force or scientific fact or claim every mode of accomplishing an effect are problematic (citing O'Reilly v. Morse, The Telephone Cases). Applications that are sensorially verifiable and not merely opinion are more likely to weigh in favor of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether a general concept (principle/theory/plan/scheme) is involved in executing the steps of the method
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of such a general concept can be a clue that the claim is drawn to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant factors: (a) extent to which use of the concept would preempt its use in other fields; (b) extent to which the claim is abstract/sweeping covering known and unknown uses and any machinery; (c) extent to which the claim would cover all possible solutions to a problem (statement of problem vs specific solution); (d) whether the concept is disembodied or well-instantiated (instantiated concepts weigh in favor). A concept that is not well-instantiated weighs against eligibility (citing Bilski, Diehr, Research Corp., DealerTrack, Ultramercial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism(s) by which the steps are implemented (observability/verifiability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the performance of the process is observable and verifiable rather than subjective or imperceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps that are observable and verifiable weigh in favor of eligibility (citing The Telephone Cases and Tilghman v. Proctor). The mechanism(s) of implementation (how steps are carried out) can influence whether the claim is a practical application or merely a mental/abstract formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of general concepts (non-exhaustive list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of general concepts include, but are not limited to: basic economic practices or theories; basic legal theories; mathematical concepts; mental activity; interpersonal interactions; teaching concepts; human behavior; instructing 'how business should be conducted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories as heuristics to identify claims that may be drawing to abstract ideas (citations: Bilski, Benson, Ferguson, Le Roy). They are examples, not an exclusive list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making the determination of eligibility (weighing factors; examiner documentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each relevant factor should be weighed to determine whether the method is claiming an abstract idea by covering a general concept or whether it is limited to a particular practical application. The presence or absence of a single factor will not be determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factors indicate the method claim is not merely covering an abstract idea, the claim is eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101 and must be further evaluated under 102, 103, and 112. If factors indicate the claim attempts to cover an abstract idea, the examiner will reject under 35 U.S.C. 101, providing clear rationale and specifically pointing out the factors relied upon so the applicant can respond. The examiner's conclusion must be based on the evidence as a whole. Under compact prosecution, each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement in the initial review and Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish on the Record a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel should review the totality of the evidence (e.g., specification, claims, relevant prior art) before concluding whether the claimed invention is statutory or within an exception. "The examiner bears the initial burden … of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record suggests it is more likely than not that the claimed invention would be considered a practical application of an abstract idea, physical phenomenon, or law of nature, then USPTO personnel should not reject the claim. After identifying and explaining in the record the reasons why a claim is for an abstract idea/law/natural phenomenon with no practical application, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend or show why the claim is eligible (citing In re Oetiker, In re Brana).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject Matter Eligibility Analysis of Process Claims Involving Laws of Nature — essential three inquiries (MPEP § 2106.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining what applicant invented and establishing the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention, conduct the following three inquiries on the claim as a whole: (1) Is the claimed invention directed to a process (an act or series of acts or steps)? (2) Does the claim focus on use of a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or naturally occurring relation or correlation (is the natural principle a limiting feature)? (3) Does the claim include additional elements/steps or a combination that integrate the natural principle into the claimed invention such that the natural principle is practically applied and the claim amounts to significantly more than the natural principle itself?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Inquiry 1 is No, this analysis is not applicable (see MPEP § 2106 for products). If Inquiry 2 is No, analyze instead whether an abstract idea is claimed (MPEP § 2106). If Inquiry 3 is No (i.e., the claim is no more than the natural principle plus instructions to apply it), the claim is not patent-eligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. The guidance emphasizes integration of the natural principle into a practical application and that mere application without significantly more is insufficient.
